source.title: Baby Llama: knowledge distillation from an ensemble of teachers trained on a small dataset with no performance penalty

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Reports outcomes bearing on scaling with model size and on whether evaluation loss predicts benchmark performance, but does not fit or reproduce the original scaling-law analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper cites compute-optimal scaling as context but does not test power-law fits, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocations, or architectural invariance. Its own Switch Transformer scaling result and its statements about evaluation loss and benchmark performance bear on V1 and V6. Other benchmark comparisons are not extracted separately because the paper reports an aggregate comparison relevant to V6.
record.test_reason: The paper is a BabyLM distillation study. It cites the Chinchilla scaling law only as motivation and in its limitations. It fits no power law, sweeps no scale axis and does not examine compute-optimal allocation. None of its results measures what any version names: the Switch Transformer note concerns mixture-of-experts expert count in a data-bottlenecked regime, the student-beats-teachers result concerns distillation, and the eval-loss remark is an unquantified aside about hyperparameter tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the 58M LLaMA distilled from a GPT-2 705M plus LLaMA 360M ensemble outperforms the same model trained conventionally, both teachers and their logit ensemble. They caution that results at this small scale and parameters-exceed-tokens regime may not generalize to large models.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates small language models using ensemble distillation and selected architecture comparisons; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: Switch Transformer loss worsened as expert count and capacity increased. The authors also state that evaluation loss was not a sufficiently reliable proxy for benchmark performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing Switch Transformer expert count and capacity on a 10M-word dataset degraded loss and zero-shot scores, even with longer training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-bottlenecked tiny-corpus regimes, adding mixture-of-experts parameters does not lower loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Across distillation hyperparameter settings, eval loss did not correlate well enough with benchmarks to serve as a proxy (no numbers given).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a fixed model size, variation in eval loss across training hyperparameters is a poor proxy for benchmark score in small-data regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: A 58M distilled student beats its 360M and 705M teachers and their ensemble on most BLiMP tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation from larger teachers trained on a small dataset can exceed teacher downstream performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the BabyLM Challenge at the 27th Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning
record.problems: The Switch Transformer result has no numerical loss values or stated parameter counts. The evaluation-loss/benchmark observation has no numerical correlation or specified model set. The authors report no systematic hyperparameter search and caution that their models are much smaller than current state-of-the-art models.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained for the many individual zero-shot benchmark scores in Appendix A, Table 1; R2 records the aggregate comparison explicitly stated in the text. Fine-tuning and age-of-acquisition scores do not report a relationship with scale or pretraining loss.
record.verdict_notes: Table 1 does contain undistilled LLaMA 58M, LLaMA 360M and GPT-2 705M on BLiMP, but these differ in architecture and epochs and were all trained in a regime where data is the bottleneck. The paper does not present them as a scaling comparison, so I added no rows. The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V1 'challenges' and V6 'limits_scope' labels are not supported.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or exponent; no sweep across several orders of magnitude, tokens, or compute.
No systematic scaling curve or quantified relationship across controlled model sizes; evaluation loss and benchmark correlation is reported without numerical results.

rows.subject: Switch Transformers (different expert configurations; aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of experts and expert capacity; allowed longer training for larger configurations.

conditions.value: number of experts and expert capacity increased
larger models were allowed longer training

rows.baseline: A Switch Transformer with one expert of capacity 1 closely matches the GPT2-10M baseline.
rows.value: The authors report degradation in loss as the number of experts and expert capacity increase.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the configurations tested; parameter counts and individual loss values are not stated.
rows.check: This is an appendix side experiment on mixture-of-experts expert count and capacity, with GPT2-10M-sized backbones on 10M words. Parameters far exceed tokens, so data is the bottleneck, which V1 explicitly excludes. Expert count is not total-parameter scaling at a non-bottlenecked budget. No loss values or parameter counts are given. It cannot bear on V1, and 'reversed' is not justified.

rows.subject: Baby Llama (58M, distilled)
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero-shot benchmark accuracy with the two teacher models and their logit-averaged ensemble.

conditions.value: BLiMP and supplementary zero-shot benchmarks; aggregate statement
LLaMA (360M), GPT-2 (705M), and ensemble of teachers

rows.baseline: The two individual teachers and their ensemble; per-task values are listed in Appendix A, Table 1.
rows.value: Baby Llama performs better than both individual teachers on most zero-shot tasks and also outperforms the teacher ensemble.
rows.note: The text gives this aggregate comparison; the table lists separate scores by task.
rows.check: This compares the study's own distilled student with its teachers, i.e. the paper's method against others. It is not a scale-versus-downstream test. The training regimes differ (distillation vs standard; different epochs and architectures). It should not count as evidence on V6.

rows.subject: Evaluated language models (aggregate; exact set not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Assessed whether evaluation loss could serve as a proxy for benchmark performance.
rows.measure: relationship between evaluation loss and benchmark performance
rows.value: The authors state that evaluation loss did not correlate sufficiently well with benchmark results to be used as a proxy for final model performance.
rows.note: The paper provides no correlation coefficient, model list, or numerical loss results for this observation.
rows.check: This is an anecdotal remark made while tuning distillation hyperparameters. There is no model set, no numbers and no variation in scale. It does not measure downstream improvement with scale or with pretraining loss across models of different size, so it cannot be scored against V6.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
